title: Stretch, Salt and a Steady Filter
endLine: Stretch and salt signals tune the afferent arteriole, keeping filtration nearly steady.

scenes.tts: Two tiny arterioles set the kidney filter's pressure and its flow. But the arterial pressure feeding them changes. How does filtration stay nearly steady?
scenes.narration: Two tiny arterioles set the kidney filter's pressure and its flow. But the arterial pressure feeding them changes. How does filtration stay nearly steady?
scenes.caption: Two tiny arterioles set the kidney filter's pressure and its flow. But the arterial pressure feeding them changes. How does filtration stay nearly steady?
scenes.visual: Continue the first film's 16:9 world and colour map without a reset: one straight glomerular capillary across the middle of the frame, the GREEN afferent arteriole with its tap ring on the left, the YELLOW efferent arteriole with its nozzle on the right, RED plasma dots flowing left to right with a broad red flow arrow, PURPLE protein dots, CYAN filtrate drops falling into the pale BLUE 'Bowman's space' band beneath; all text WHITE; the small 'schematic' tag stays at bottom right throughout. The first film's orange-and-purple push-pull strip shows faintly above the tube during the first sentence, then fades out for this film. New carried object: at the far left, on the inflow, a WHITE dial gauge labelled 'arterial pressure'. On 'Two tiny arterioles', the green ring and then the yellow ring pulse. On 'changes', the dial needle starts swinging slowly up and down and keeps swinging for most of the film. On the question, white text across the top: 'Steady filtration?' Both the RED dots flowing through and the CYAN drops under the tube keep an even pace despite the swinging needle.
Title 'Stretch, Salt and a Steady Filter' fades in above the tube for 2 s while the dial needle keeps swinging and drops keep falling evenly; 'Steady filtration?' fades out beneath it.

scenes.tts: In mammals, kidney blood flow and filtration stay nearly constant. That holds over perfusion pressures of about 80 to 180 millimeters of mercury. On a graph, it is a long, nearly flat stretch. This is autoregulation. Two mechanisms do most of it, both acting mainly on the afferent arteriole.
scenes.narration: In mammals, kidney blood flow and filtration stay nearly constant. That holds over perfusion pressures of about 80 to 180 mmHg. On a graph, it is a long, nearly flat stretch. This is autoregulation. Two mechanisms do most of it, both acting mainly on the afferent arteriole.
scenes.caption: In mammals, kidney blood flow and filtration stay nearly constant. That holds over perfusion pressures of about 80 to 180 mmHg. On a graph, it is a long, nearly flat stretch. This is autoregulation. Two mechanisms do most of it, both acting mainly on the afferent arteriole.
scenes.visual: A graph opens in the space above the tube (the tube stays across the middle, still large): horizontal axis 'perfusion pressure (mmHg)' with ticks at 80 and 180, vertical axis 'flow and filtration'. A CYAN line draws across: nearly flat between 80 and 180, sloping outside that range. Only the 80 and 180 marks come from the lesson; the plateau height and the slopes outside the range are schematic. The dial needle now swings between 80 and 180, and a white dot rides along the flat part of the line in step with it. On 'autoregulation', that word appears above the flat part. On 'afferent arteriole', the GREEN ring glows and two small empty white tags appear beside it, numbered '1' and '2'. At the end of the scene the graph shrinks away to a small icon in the top-left corner.

scenes.tts: The first reads stretch. When rising pressure stretches the arteriole's smooth muscle, the muscle depolarizes. Calcium inside it rises, and it contracts. This is the myogenic response, which Bayliss described in arteries in 1902. What senses the stretch is still debated.
scenes.narration: The first reads stretch. When rising pressure stretches the arteriole's smooth muscle, the muscle depolarizes. Calcium inside it rises, and it contracts. This is the myogenic response, which Bayliss described in arteries in 1902. What senses the stretch is still debated.
scenes.caption: The first reads stretch. When rising pressure stretches the arteriole's smooth muscle, the muscle depolarizes. Calcium inside it rises, and it contracts. This is the myogenic response, which Bayliss described in arteries in 1902. What senses the stretch is still debated.
scenes.visual: Push in on the GREEN afferent arteriole until its wall fills most of the frame height; the arterial dial stays visible at the left edge. The needle rises and the green wall bulges outward, with white arrows pressing out on it, label 'stretch'. On 'depolarizes', a bright ripple runs along the green muscle band. On 'Calcium inside it rises', small WHITE specks brighten inside the wall. On 'it contracts', the wall squeezes back inward, narrowing the tube, and the RED dots passing through return to their earlier pace. Label 'myogenic response', with a small 'Bayliss, 1902' beneath it. On 'still debated', a white '?' appears beside the stretch arrows and stays. Tag '1' fills in with the word 'stretch'.

scenes.tts: The second reads the tubule instead. Each tubule comes back to touch its own glomerulus. There, at the end of the thick ascending limb, sits a plaque of cells, the macula densa. So the fluid leaving the loop can adjust filtration upstream.
scenes.narration: The second reads the tubule instead. Each tubule comes back to touch its own glomerulus. There, at the end of the thick ascending limb, sits a plaque of cells, the macula densa. So the fluid leaving the loop can adjust filtration upstream.
scenes.caption: The second reads the tubule instead. Each tubule comes back to touch its own glomerulus. There, at the end of the thick ascending limb, sits a plaque of cells, the macula densa. So the fluid leaving the loop can adjust filtration upstream.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the whole hose. The Bowman's space band now drains into a CYAN tubule that runs off to the right, loops down and back along the bottom of the frame, and rises again on the left to touch the GREEN afferent arteriole (route schematic). CYAN drops travel along it. On 'comes back to touch', the returning end of the tubule glows where it meets the green ring. On 'the macula densa', a MAGENTA patch of cells on the tubule wall at that touching point lights up, label 'macula densa'. On 'adjust filtration upstream', a white arrow runs from the magenta patch to the green ring. Objects on screen: dial, green arteriole, capillary with Bowman's space, yellow arteriole, tubule with magenta patch.

scenes.tts: More salt, sodium chloride, arriving there constricts the afferent arteriole. Less salt dilates it, and renin-secreting cells in the arteriole wall release renin. This is tubuloglomerular feedback.
scenes.narration: More salt (NaCl) arriving there constricts the afferent arteriole. Less salt dilates it, and renin-secreting cells in the arteriole wall release renin. This is tubuloglomerular feedback.
scenes.caption: More salt (NaCl) arriving there constricts the afferent arteriole. Less salt dilates it, and renin-secreting cells in the arteriole wall release renin. This is tubuloglomerular feedback.
scenes.visual: Salt appears as WHITE specks riding in the tubule fluid. On 'More salt', a dense stream of white specks reaches the magenta patch; the GREEN ring tightens, the red arrow thins and the drops from the capillary slow; label 'more salt: constrict'. On 'Less salt', a thin stream of specks arrives; the GREEN ring widens, the drops quicken, and small PINK dots labelled 'renin' puff out of the green wall; label 'less salt: dilate'. The ring then settles to its middle setting. On 'tubuloglomerular feedback', that name appears along the tubule loop. Tag '2' beside the green ring fills in with the word 'salt'.

scenes.tts: Salt enters the macula densa cells through a carrier called N K C C two. When more arrives, the cells release A T P. Adenosine made from it acts on A one receptors. The afferent arteriole constricts, so the filter's pressure and filtration fall.
scenes.narration: Salt enters the macula densa cells through a carrier called NKCC2. When more arrives, the cells release ATP. Adenosine made from it acts on A1 receptors. The afferent arteriole constricts, so the filter's pressure and filtration fall.
scenes.caption: Salt enters the macula densa cells through a carrier called NKCC2. When more arrives, the cells release ATP. Adenosine made from it acts on A1 receptors. The afferent arteriole constricts, so the filter's pressure and filtration fall.
scenes.visual: Zoom in on the magenta patch where it touches the green arteriole. Cells are plain rounded blocks; carriers and receptors are simple labelled doors and slots, no molecular structures. On 'N K C C two', white salt specks pass through a door on the tubule side of a magenta cell, label 'NKCC2'. On 'release A T P', more specks arrive and small MAGENTA sparks leave the far side of the cell, label 'ATP'. On 'Adenosine', the sparks change into small rings as they cross the gap, label 'adenosine'; on 'A one receptors', they dock in slots on the GREEN wall, label 'A1 receptor'. On 'constricts', the green ring tightens. Zoom back out: the drops from the capillary slow and two small white down-arrows appear, labelled 'filter pressure' and 'filtration'.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea. Two signals, stretch and salt, do most of the steadying. Stretch is read in the arteriole wall, salt in the tubule. Both act mainly on one valve upstream of the filter, the afferent arteriole.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea. Two signals, stretch and salt, do most of the steadying. Stretch is read in the arteriole wall, salt in the tubule. Both act mainly on one valve upstream of the filter, the afferent arteriole.
scenes.caption: Here is the one idea. Two signals, stretch and salt, do most of the steadying. Stretch is read in the arteriole wall, salt in the tubule. Both act mainly on one valve upstream of the filter, the afferent arteriole.
scenes.visual: The full world, down-arrows gone. A white arrow labelled 'stretch' runs from the dial to the GREEN ring; a white arrow labelled 'salt' runs from the magenta patch to the GREEN ring. Each arrow pulses as it is named and the green ring pulses with it. Above the green ring: 'one valve, upstream'. The dial needle swings again; the green ring tightens as the needle rises and widens as it falls, and the CYAN drops under the tube keep an even rate. The YELLOW nozzle stays still and slightly dimmed.

scenes.tts: Diabetes puts the salt loop to a test. High plasma glucose raises filtered glucose. The proximal tubule takes back more of it, with sodium, through a carrier called S G L T two. So less salt reaches the macula densa. What happens to filtration?
scenes.narration: Diabetes puts the salt loop to a test. High plasma glucose raises filtered glucose. The proximal tubule takes back more of it, with sodium, through a carrier called SGLT2. So less salt reaches the macula densa. What happens to filtration?
scenes.caption: Diabetes puts the salt loop to a test. High plasma glucose raises filtered glucose. The proximal tubule takes back more of it, with sodium, through a carrier called SGLT2. So less salt reaches the macula densa. What happens to filtration?
scenes.visual: The dial needle steadies. GOLD dots (glucose) join the RED plasma stream in large numbers, label 'high glucose'; many gold dots ride down into Bowman's space with the cyan drops and into the tubule. On 'proximal tubule', the first stretch of the tubule gets that label and a door labelled 'SGLT2' opens in its wall: gold dots and white salt specks leave the tubule through it together. Downstream, the white specks reaching the magenta patch visibly thin out. Question card in white across the top: 'Less salt arriving: filtration?'

Predict pause. The question card 'Less salt arriving: filtration?' stays. Near-stillness by design: the green ring holds its setting, drops fall at their even rate, gold and white specks drift slowly in the tubule, the magenta patch glows faintly.

scenes.tts: It rises. With less salt arriving, the afferent arteriole dilates. Pressure in the filter climbs, and filtration with it. This is hyperfiltration. Whether blunted feedback or other upstream dilation dominates is still open.
scenes.narration: It rises. With less salt arriving, the afferent arteriole dilates. Pressure in the filter climbs, and filtration with it. This is hyperfiltration. Whether blunted feedback or other upstream dilation dominates is still open.
scenes.caption: It rises. With less salt arriving, the afferent arteriole dilates. Pressure in the filter climbs, and filtration with it. This is hyperfiltration. Whether blunted feedback or other upstream dilation dominates is still open.
scenes.visual: The card dissolves. On 'dilates', the GREEN ring widens and the red arrow broadens. On 'Pressure in the filter climbs', the CYAN drops under the tube fall faster and a white up-arrow labelled 'filtration' appears; then the label 'hyperfiltration' above the tube. On 'still open', two small white tags appear beside the green ring, 'blunted feedback?' and 'other dilation?', and both stay unconfirmed, each with a question mark.

scenes.tts: So the filter is steadied mostly at its inlet. The arteriole wall reads the pressure, and the tubule reads the salt. Both answers come back to the same upstream valve, across that wide range of pressures.
scenes.narration: So the filter is steadied mostly at its inlet. The arteriole wall reads the pressure, and the tubule reads the salt. Both answers come back to the same upstream valve, across that wide range of pressures.
scenes.caption: So the filter is steadied mostly at its inlet. The arteriole wall reads the pressure, and the tubule reads the salt. Both answers come back to the same upstream valve, across that wide range of pressures.
scenes.visual: The gold dots and the two question tags fade; the green ring returns to its middle setting and the drops return to their even rate. The dial needle swings between 80 and 180 once more. On 'reads the pressure', the 'stretch' arrow from the dial pulses; on 'reads the salt', the 'salt' arrow from the magenta patch pulses; on 'the same upstream valve', both arrows pulse together into the GREEN ring, which tightens and widens in counter-step with the needle while the drops stay even.

End card over the dimmed but still moving world, large white text, centred: 'Stretch and salt signals tune the afferent arteriole, keeping filtration nearly steady.' Behind it the dial needle swings gently, the green ring answers, and cyan drops fall at an even rate.
